query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The coupled response of high-entropy alloys to tribo-corrosion is governed by the formation of a protective oxide layer, which acts as a barrier against further oxidation and wear.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy with a single-phase or multi-phase microstructure
generation.intervention: Tribo-corrosion, involving both wear and corrosion
generation.conditions: Harsh environments, such as high temperatures, corrosive media, and mechanical stress
generation.structural_mediator: Protective oxide layer, such as chromia (Cr2O3) or alumina (Al2O3)
generation.mechanism: The protective oxide layer forms on the surface of the high-entropy alloy, reducing the rate of oxidation and wear by acting as a diffusion barrier
generation.predicted_outcome: The high-entropy alloy will exhibit improved resistance to tribo-corrosion, with reduced wear and corrosion rates, compared to a baseline alloy without the protective oxide layer
generation.baseline: A high-entropy alloy without a protective oxide layer, or a conventional alloy with poor corrosion resistance
generation.boundary: The protective oxide layer may break down or become unstable under extreme conditions, such as very high temperatures or corrosive media, leading to accelerated wear and corrosion
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and microstructure of the high-entropy alloy, as well as the specific conditions of the tribo-corrosion test, may influence the formation and stability of the protective oxide layer

falsification_experiment.design: Tribo-corrosion test of a high-entropy alloy with a controlled composition and microstructure, compared to a baseline alloy
measurements: Protective oxide layer thickness and composition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy exhibits no improvement in resistance to tribo-corrosion, or if the protective oxide layer is not formed or is unstable, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. As a result, precipitation strengthening should be considered in developing HEAs for high temperature applications. Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
